citations.quote: Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be a countably generated measurable space ([[def-measurable-space]]), $P$ a probability kernel ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and $\phi$ a nonzero $\sigma$-finite measure ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) on $\mathcal X$. Write $P^n$ for the $n$-fold kernel iterate. The kernel is **$\phi$-irreducible** if, for every $A\in\mathcal X$ with $\phi(A)>0$ and every $x\in\mathsf X$, there is an integer $n\ge1$ such that $P^n(x,A)>0$. Equivalently, the sum of these nonnegative probabilities over $n\ge1$ is positive. No recurrence or invariant law is part of this definition.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

Assume Choice. For every probability measure $\mu$ and probability kernel $K$
on an arbitrary measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$, the canonical path space
$$ (E^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}) $$
carries a unique probability $\mathbb P_\mu$ under which the coordinate maps
form a Markov chain with initial law $\mu$ and transition kernel $K$.

Assume Choice. Let $X$ be a $K$-chain, let
$\tau:\Omega\to\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$ be a stopping time, and let $H$ be a
bounded measurable path functional. Put $h(x)=\mathbb E_xH$ and define the
everywhere meaningful random variables
$$ Z_H:=\sum_{n\ge0}1_{\{\tau=n\}}H(X_n,X_{n+1},\ldots), \qquad R_h:=\sum_{n\ge0}1_{\{\tau=n\}}h(X_n). $$ Both are defined to be zero on $\{\tau=\infty\}$. Then $$ \mathbb E[Z_H\mid\mathcal F_\tau]=R_h\quad\text{a.s.} $$ This is the precise meaning of the usual eventwise notation $$ \mathbb E[1_{\{\tau<\infty\}}H(X_\tau,X_{\tau+1},\ldots)\mid\mathcal F_\tau] =1_{\{\tau<\infty\}}h(X_\tau): $$
no value $X_\infty$ is used. If $\tau<\infty$ almost surely, the indicators can
be omitted.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: For the additional conclusion, let $f(x)=\sum_{n\ge1}P^n(x,A)$. By [F1], $f(x)>0$ everywhere. Tonelli and stationarity give $\int f\,d\pi=\sum_{n\ge1}\pi(A)$. If $\pi(A)=0$, this integral is zero, contradicting positivity of $f$ under a probability measure. Hence $\pi(A)>0$; [F1] also supplies the positive-hitting premise for the first assertion.

It remains to prove the first assertion under its positive-hitting premise. Set $q_0=1_A$ and recursively $q_{n+1}=1_A+1_{A^c}Pq_n$, where $Pq_n(x)=\int q_n(y)P(x,dy)$. Then $q_n(x)=\Pr_x(\tau_A\le n)$; induction and [F7] show each $q_n$ is measurable, and $q_n\uparrow q:=\Pr_x(\tau_A<\infty)$, so $q$ is measurable. If the bad set $\{q<1\}$ has positive mass, a countable level-set union gives some $\delta_1>0$ for which $B_1=\{x:q(x)\le1-\delta_1\}$ has positive $\pi$-measure. For each $x\in B_1$, $q(x)>0$ and $x\notin A$, so some $\ell_0\ge1$ has $P^{\ell_0}(x,A)>0$. Countable unions over times and rational thresholds then give a common $\ell_0\ge1$, $\delta_2>0$, and $B_2\subseteq B_1$ with $\pi(B_2)>0$ and $P^{\ell_0}(x,A)\ge\delta_2$ on $B_2$.

Let $\eta=\#\{k\ge1:X_{k\ell_0}\in B_2\}$. At each such visit, the conditional probability of avoiding $A$ at the next $\ell_0$-step time is at most $1-\delta_2$. Induction using [F4] gives $\Pr_x(\tau_A=\infty,\eta\ge r)\le(1-\delta_2)^r$ for each finite $r$, and hence $\Pr_x(\tau_A=\infty,\eta=\infty)=0$. Thus for $x\in B_2$, $\Pr_x(\tau_A=\infty,\eta<\infty)\ge\delta_1$. To select a measurable positive-mass set with a common finite last-visit bound, for each $\ell\ge1$ forbid $A$ at every time and also forbid $B_2$ at times $k\ell_0$ with $k\ge\ell$. For a finite horizon $N$, let $F_n^{(\ell)}=A\cup B_2$ if $n=k\ell_0$ for some $k\ge\ell$, and $F_n^{(\ell)}=A$ otherwise. Set $g_{N,N}=1_{(F_N^{(\ell)})^c}$ and recursively set $g_{N,n}=1_{(F_n^{(\ell)})^c}Pg_{N,n+1}$ for $n=N-1,\ldots,0$. Then $g_{\ell,N}=g_{N,0}$ is the finite-horizon event probability and is measurable by [F7]. As $N\to\infty$, these events decrease to $\{\tau_A=\infty,\sup\{k\ge1:X_{k\ell_0}\in B_2\}<\ell\}$, so continuity from above makes their limit $g_\ell(x)$ measurable. The events increase with $\ell$ and their union is $\{\tau_A=\infty,\eta<\infty\}$, so $g_\ell(x)\uparrow$ a value at least $\delta_1$ on $B_2$. A countable rational threshold selection therefore gives $\ell\ge1$, $\delta>0$, and $B\subseteq B_2$ with $\pi(B)>0$ and $\Pr_x\!\left(\tau_A=\infty,\ \sup\{k\ge1:X_{k\ell_0}\in B_2\}<\ell\right)\ge\delta\quad(x\in B).$

Put $L=\ell\ell_0$ and $S=\sup\{k\ge1:X_{kL}\in B\}$, with $S=-\infty$ if no such visit occurs. For $1\le r\le j$, consider the event that $X_{rL}\in B$, there is no later $B$-visit at a positive multiple of $L$, and no hit of $A$ at or after $rL$. It is a subset of $\{S=r,\ X_{jL}\notin A\}$. Stationarity and the Markov property at time $rL$ therefore give $\Pr_\pi(S=r,\ X_{jL}\notin A)\ge\int_B\pi(dy)\Pr_y(\tau_A=\infty,\ S=-\infty)\ge\pi(B)\delta.$ Indeed the event in step 2.1 rules out every $B_2$-visit at skeleton indices $k\ge\ell$, hence every later $B$-visit at a positive multiple of $L=\ell\ell_0$, as well as every future hit of $A$. The events $S=r$ are disjoint, so stationarity yields $\pi(A^c)\ge j\pi(B)\delta$. Taking $j>1/(\pi(B)\delta)$ contradicts $\pi(A^c)\le1$. Therefore the bad set is $\pi$-null.

For a probability kernel $P$ on $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), a measurable set $C$ is **$(m,\epsilon,\nu)$-small** if $m\ge1$ is an integer, $0<\epsilon\le1$, $\nu$ is a probability measure ([[def-probability-measure]]), and
$$P^m(x,A)\ge\epsilon\nu(A)\quad(x\in C,\ A\in\mathcal X).$$
The inequality is pointwise in $x$ and holds for every measurable $A$.

A **geometric drift inequality outside $C$** consists of a finite-valued measurable $V:\mathsf X\to[1,\infty)$, constants $0<\lambda<1$ and $0\le b<\infty$, and
$$PV(x):=\int V(y)P(x,dy)\le\lambda V(x)+b\,1_C(x)\quad(x\in\mathsf X).$$
The terms small set and drift are separate hypotheses; neither definition asserts the existence of the other.

When an invariant probability $\pi$ is specified ([[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]), an **extended geometric drift certificate finite $\pi$-almost everywhere** allows measurable $V:\mathsf X\to[1,+\infty]$ with $\pi(V<\infty)=1$ and the same pointwise inequality, interpreted in the nonnegative extended reals. This is a separate convention from the finite-valued drift function above. The geometric theorem treats this certificate on $E=\{V<\infty\}$; the original finite-valued convention gives the corresponding bound on the whole state space.

Let $P$ have invariant probability $\pi$. If a measurable set $A$ has positive probability of being hit from every starting state, then $\Pr_x(\tau_A<\infty)=1$ for $\pi$-almost every $x$. In addition, if $P$ is $\phi$-irreducible and $\phi(A)>0$, then $\pi(A)>0$ and the positive-hitting hypothesis holds.
Suppose $C$ is $(m,\epsilon,\nu)$-small and $PV\le\lambda V+b1_C$ with finite $V\ge1$, $0<\lambda<1$. For every finite $d\ge1$, $D=C\cup\{V\le d\}$ is petite.

Let $P$ be countably generated, $\phi$-irreducible and aperiodic with invariant probability $\pi$. Suppose $D$ is petite with probability $
u$ and multiplier $\alpha>0$, and $C\subseteq D$ is $(m,\epsilon,
u)$-small for this same $
u$, with $
u(C)>0$ and $
u\ll\pi$. Then $D$ is small at some common time.

u\ll\pi$ be a probability. Suppose every state has some $n(x)\ge1$ and $\delta(x)>0$ with $P^{n(x)}(x,\cdot)\ge\delta(x)
u(\cdot)$. Then there is $N$ such that for every $n\ge N$, $
u P^n\ge\epsilon_n
u$ for some $\epsilon_n>0$.

Let $P$ be a $\phi$-irreducible probability kernel ([[def-phi-irreducible-chain]]) with invariant probability $\pi$ ([[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]). The chain is **aperiodic** if there do not exist an integer $d\ge2$ and pairwise disjoint measurable sets $X_1,\ldots,X_d$ such that $\pi(X_1)>0$ and
$$P(x,X_{i+1})=1\quad(x\in X_i,\ 1\le i<d),\qquad P(x,X_1)=1\quad(x\in X_d).$$
Invariance then gives $\pi(X_i)>0$ for every $i$. The sets need not cover the full state space; the definition rules out any positive-mass cyclic part. Aperiodicity does not itself assert convergence.

([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The

measures evaluated at $A$.

$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

Let $P$ be countably generated, $\phi$-irreducible and aperiodic with invariant probability $\pi$. Suppose $C$ is $(m,\epsilon,
u)$-small with $\phi(C)>0$ and $PV\le\lambda V+b1_C$ for finite $V\ge1$, $0<\lambda<1$. Then there are $\lambda'\in(\lambda,1)$ and a $\phi$-positive small set $C_0\subseteq C$ with $\sup_{C_0}V<\infty$ and $PV\le\lambda'V+b1_{C_0}$ pointwise. Moreover there are a bounded-$V$ small set $D$, a time $L$, a minorizing probability $
u'$, and $a<1$ such that for $Q=P^L$ and $h(x,y)=(V(x)+V(y))/2$,
$$Q\otimes Q\,h\le ah\quad	ext{off }D^2.$$
If $Q(x,\cdot)\ge\epsilon_D
u'$ on $D$, the residual laws $R_x=(Q(x,\cdot)-\epsilon_D
u')/(1-\epsilon_D)$ have $\sup_{x,y\in D}R_x\otimes R_y(h)<\infty$ when $\epsilon_D<1$; for $\epsilon_D=1$ no residual branch is needed.

Let $Q$ be a probability kernel, $D$ be $(1,\epsilon,\nu)$-small for $Q$, and let $0<a<1$. If $0<\epsilon<1$, define residual probabilities $R_x=(Q(x,\cdot)-\epsilon\nu)/(1-\epsilon)$ on $D$ and assume
$$B\ge\max\{1,(1-\epsilon)\sup_{(x,y)\in D^2}R_x\otimes R_y(h)/a\}<\infty.$$
If $\epsilon=1$, set $B=1$ and impose no residual condition. Suppose $h:\mathsf X^2\to[1,\infty)$ is finite-valued and measurable and $Q\otimes Q\,h\le ah$ off $D^2$. Then there are $M<\infty$ and $0<r<1$ such that a coupling of two $Q$-chains satisfies
$$\Pr_{x,y}(X_n\ne Y_n)\le M h(x,y)r^n.$$
For $\epsilon=1$, the first visit to $D^2$ couples the chains immediately.
Let $\pi$ be invariant for $P$, and suppose $PV\le\lambda V+b1_C$ with $V\ge1$, $0<\lambda<1$, and $\sup_CV<\infty$. Then $\pi V<\infty$.

If $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable and $\int f\,d\mu<+\infty$, then
$f(x)<+\infty$ for almost every $x$.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $P$ have invariant probability $\pi$. If a measurable set $A$ has positive probability of being hit from every starting state, then $\Pr_x(\tau_A<\infty)=1$ for $\pi$-almost every $x$. In addition, if $P$ is $\phi$-irreducible and $\phi(A)>0$, then $\pi(A)>0$ and the positive-hitting hypothesis holds.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: First assume $V$ is finite-valued. By [F6], choose the bounded-$V$ small subset $C_0$ and $\lambda'\in(\lambda,1)$ with $PV\le\lambda'V+b1_{C_0}$. Its boundedness is exactly the hypothesis needed for [F8], which now gives $\pi V<\infty$. Apply the remaining conclusions of [F6] to obtain a skeleton $Q=P^L$, bounded small set $D$, function $h(x,y)=(V(x)+V(y))/2$, and constants satisfying the hypotheses of [F7]. Since $D$ is bounded in $V$, the residual split expectation is uniformly finite.

By [F7], for the initial pair $(x,Y_0)$ with $Y_0\sim\pi$, the coupling disagreement at skeleton time $k$ is at most $M_0h(x,Y_0)r_0^k$. The finite invariant moment from step 1.1 gives $\mathbb E h(x,Y_0)=\tfrac12(V(x)+\pi V)\le\tfrac12(1+\pi V)V(x).$ The coupling inequality [F5] yields a $V(x)$-weighted geometric bound along skeleton times.

Write $n=Lk+s$, $0\le s<L$. The finite set of residual powers $P^s$ contracts total variation and the stationary law remains $\pi$. Absorb the finite factor and $r_0^{-s/L}$ over $s=0,\ldots,L-1$ into a single $M$, and put $r=r_0^{1/L}$. Then the asserted bound holds for every $n$.

Now allow the extended certificate and put $N=\{V=+\infty\}$ and $E=N^c$. These sets are measurable and $\pi(N)=0$. If $x\in E$, the pointwise drift bound has finite right side, so $PV(x)<\infty$. Apply [F9] to $V$ under the probability measure $P(x,\cdot)$ to obtain $P(x,N)=0$. Thus $E$ is absorbing, including for every iterate. Also $\phi(N)=0$: otherwise [F10] would give $\pi(N)>0$. Hence $\phi(C\cap E)=\phi(C)>0$, in particular $C\cap E$ is nonempty, and $\phi|_E$ remains a nonzero sigma-finite irreducibility measure.

Restrict the state space to $E$ with its trace sigma-algebra and set $P_E(x,A)=P(x,A)$ for trace-measurable $A\subseteq E$. Absorption makes this a probability kernel, with invariant probability $\pi|_E$; a countable generator of $\mathcal X$ restricts to a countable generator on $E$. Original irreducibility supplies positive finite-time access to every positive-$\phi|_E$ set from each $x\in E$. For the original $(m,\epsilon,
u)$-minorization on $C$, choose $x\in C\cap E$. Since $P^m(x,N)=0$, minorization gives $
u(N)=0$, so $C\cap E$ is small for $P_E$ with probability $
u|_E$. Any positive-$\pi|_E$ cyclic part for $P_E$ would consist of original measurable subsets of $E$ with the same pointwise transitions under $P$, contradicting the actual aperiodicity definition [F2], which excludes such a part without requiring it to cover the state space. Finally $V|_E$ is finite-valued and satisfies the original drift inequality with drift set $C\cap E$.

Apply the finite-valued result proved in steps 1.1–2.1 to $(E,P_E,\phi|_E,\pi|_E,V|_E,C\cap E)$. It gives constants $M<\infty$ and $0<r<1$ and the weighted bound for every $x\in E$. Both $P^n(x,\cdot)$ and $\pi$ are supported on $E$, so their total variation on the original space equals their total variation on the trace space: every event is replaced by its intersection with $E$. Thus precisely the displayed original-space bound holds on $E$, a full-$\pi$ absorbing set. If $V$ is globally finite, $E=\mathsf X$ and the first branch is recovered.
